About This Part
Volume 8D develops production judgment for containerized and event-driven application platforms on Google
Cloud. The objective is not to deploy a sample and stop. It is to build a trustworthy software supply chain, select
the right runtime, design identity and networking, control traffic and concurrency, engineer asynchronous
delivery, and prove recovery under failure. The chapters progress from artifact integrity to Kubernetes, serverless containers, functions, APIs, messaging,
event routing, and workflow orchestration. Each lab requires measurable evidence, least-privilege identities,
controlled rollout, observability, failure testing, and cleanup. Volume 8 Progress

Platform Safety and Cost Controls

Use an isolated project, budgets, quotas, small clusters, short-lived revisions, and explicit deletion steps. GKE
nodes, load balancers, NAT, Artifact Registry storage, Apigee, and networking resources can continue
charging after a lab ends.

Never download long-lived service-account keys for runtime workloads. Prefer Workload Identity
Federation for GKE, attached service identities, and short-lived federation for CI/CD.



Use immutable image digests, vulnerability evidence, staged promotion, policy enforcement, and rollback. A
successful image build is not evidence that an artifact is authorized or safe to run.

Assume at-least-once delivery unless a documented service guarantee and end-to-end design prove
otherwise. Consumers must be idempotent and poison messages must be isolated.

Distinguish synchronous request paths, asynchronous queues, event routing, scheduled triggers, and
durable orchestration. Selecting the wrong primitive creates reliability and cost problems. Table of Contents

Chapter 31 - Artifact Registry and Container Supply-Chain
Engineering
Building immutable, attestable, and policy-controlled software delivery
Learning Objectives

Design Artifact Registry repositories, identities, retention, and regional placement.

Build and promote images by digest instead of mutable tags.

Integrate vulnerability scanning, provenance, SBOMs, signing, and Binary Authorization.

Operate artifact lifecycle, incident response, and rollback.
31.1 Repository Architecture and Trust Boundaries
Artifact Registry stores container images and language packages in regional or multi-regional repositories. Repository boundaries should reflect ownership, environment, residency, promotion, and access. Avoid one
global writeable repository shared by every team and environment. Pattern

31.2 Immutable Build and Promotion
Tags are convenient human references but can move. Production deployment records should resolve to
immutable digests. Build once, test once, and promote the same digest through environments.

Immutable Build and Promotion
Tags are convenient human references but can move. Production deployment records should resolve to
immutable digests. Build once, test once, and promote the same digest through environments. Rebuilding from
the same source can produce different bytes because dependencies, base images, timestamps, and build systems
change.

Pin base images and critical dependencies.

Record source revision, builder identity, build parameters, digest, test evidence, and approvals.

Separate build identity from deploy identity.

Require pull-only access for runtimes and restricted write access for trusted pipelines.
gcloud artifacts repositories list --location=REGION
gcloud artifacts docker images list REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/platform --include-tags
docker pull REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/platform/orders@sha256:DIGEST
31.3 Vulnerability, Provenance, and Policy
Container Analysis and related security tooling can surface vulnerabilities and metadata. Supply-chain controls
should combine scanning, provenance, software bill of materials, signatures or attestations, and deployment
policy. Binary Authorization can prevent untrusted images from reaching GKE and supported deployment
targets.

Retention policies, cleanup rules, tag immutability conventions, and access logs prevent repositories from
becoming uncontrolled archives. During a supply-chain incident, identify affected digests, stop promotion,
revoke compromised identities, deny deployment, roll back to a known-good digest, rebuild from trusted inputs,
and preserve evidence. Troubleshooting Matrix

Prerequisites

Artifact Registry, Cloud Build or another trusted builder, a small test runtime, and permissions for
repository and policy configuration. Implementation
1. Create separate development and production repositories with least-privilege writer and reader roles.
2. Build a small application from a pinned base image and record source revision and digest.
3. Generate vulnerability and SBOM evidence; classify findings by exploitability and runtime exposure.
4. Promote the exact digest to production without rebuilding it.
5. Create an attestation or signing step and configure a policy that rejects an unsigned test image.

VOLUME 8D | 6
6. Deploy the approved digest and demonstrate rollback to the prior digest.
7. Configure cleanup rules and export audit evidence. Validation Evidence

The same digest is traceable across build, test, promotion, and deployment.

An unapproved artifact is denied while an approved artifact deploys.

Runtime identity can pull but cannot overwrite images.

Rollback and repository cleanup are proven. Cleanup

Delete test images, repositories if dedicated, policy objects, service accounts, builds, and runtime resources. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why deploy by digest?
A digest identifies immutable content; a tag can be moved and does not by itself prove which bytes were
deployed.
2. Does a vulnerability scan prove an image is safe?
No. It covers known findings in scanned components and must be combined with provenance, configuration,
exposure analysis, and policy.
3. What is Binary Authorization?
A deploy-time policy control that evaluates attestations and rules before allowing an image to run.
4. Why separate build and deploy identities?
It limits blast radius and prevents one compromised identity from both creating and releasing artifacts. Chapter Summary

Artifact integrity begins before deployment.

Build once and promote immutable digests.

Scanning, provenance, signing, and policy answer different trust questions.

Repository lifecycle and incident response require operational ownership.

Chapter 32 - Google Kubernetes Engine Architecture and Cluster
Design
Selecting GKE modes, designing cluster boundaries, and securing workload identity
Learning Objectives

Compare GKE Autopilot and Standard operating models.

Design cluster, project, region, release-channel, and tenancy boundaries.

Use Workload Identity Federation for GKE and least-privilege Kubernetes authorization.

Plan node, control-plane, upgrade, and availability architecture.
32.1 Autopilot and Standard
GKE Autopilot is a mode where Google manages node infrastructure configuration, scaling, security defaults,
and many operational settings. Standard provides deeper control of nodes, system configuration, and
specialized workloads. Modern GKE also allows selected Autopilot-mode workloads in Standard clusters
through ComputeClasses, but platform teams should adopt such features only after compatibility and lifecycle
review. Decision Area

32.2 Cluster and Tenancy Boundaries
A cluster is a security, availability, quota, upgrade, and blast-radius boundary. Separate clusters when
workloads require incompatible trust, lifecycle, networking, compliance, or operational ownership.

nancy Boundaries
A cluster is a security, availability, quota, upgrade, and blast-radius boundary. Separate clusters when
workloads require incompatible trust, lifecycle, networking, compliance, or operational ownership. Namespaces improve organization and policy but do not automatically provide hard multi-tenancy.

Prefer regional clusters for production availability where cost and service support allow.

Use separate projects and folders to reinforce billing, IAM, quota, and policy boundaries.

Choose release channels and maintenance windows deliberately.

Document which teams own cluster, namespaces, platform add-ons, and application resources.
32.3 Identity and Authorization
Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended way for workloads to access Google Cloud APIs
without downloaded service-account keys. Autopilot enables it by default; Standard requires cluster and node-
pool configuration. Kubernetes RBAC controls Kubernetes API actions, while Google Cloud IAM controls Google
Cloud resources. Both must be least-privileged.

32.4 Availability and Upgrade Design
Control-plane availability does not guarantee application availability. Applications need topology spread,
multiple replicas, PodDisruptionBudgets, readiness probes, graceful termination, suitable storage, and
dependency resilience. Release channels, surge upgrades, maintenance exclusions, and version-skew rules must
be integrated with application testing. Troubleshooting Matrix





VOLUME 8D | 9
Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. When is Autopilot a strong default?
When workloads fit supported constraints and the team benefits from Google-managed nodes and stronger
managed defaults.
2. Why are namespaces not complete tenant isolation?
Cluster-level resources, kernel/node sharing, privileged controls, and administration remain shared.
3. What does Workload Identity Federation for GKE solve?
It gives Kubernetes workloads short-lived, identity-based access to Google Cloud APIs without static keys.
4. Why use a regional cluster?
It distributes the control plane and, with suitable node placement, improves resilience to a zonal failure. Chapter Summary

Choose GKE mode from workload and operating-model evidence.

Treat cluster boundaries as security and failure boundaries.

Kubernetes RBAC and Google Cloud IAM are complementary.

Application availability must be engineered above the control plane.

Chapter 33 - GKE Production Operations, Networking, Scaling, and
Fleets
Operating Kubernetes as a controlled multi-team production platform
Learning Objectives

Engineer GKE networking, ingress, Gateway API, DNS, and network policy.

Design horizontal, vertical, cluster, and node autoscaling with failure-state capacity.

Operate upgrades, observability, backup, policy, and fleet-level governance.

Troubleshoot Kubernetes systematically from user symptom to infrastructure evidence.
33.1 Networking and Application Delivery
GKE networking spans pod and service address allocation, VPC routing, load balancing, DNS, egress, private
access, and policy. Gateway API provides role-oriented traffic management and is increasingly preferred for
advanced L7 designs, while Ingress remains common. Network Policy controls pod traffic but must be paired
with VPC firewall and identity controls. Layer

Horizontal Pod Autoscaling reacts to workload metrics; Vertical Pod Autoscaling recommends or adjusts
resource requests; cluster and node-pool autoscaling supply capacity. Scaling loops have delays and can conflict.

Prerequisites

A small GKE cluster, Artifact Registry image, metrics, and permissions for load balancing and policy. Implementation
1. Deploy a versioned application using a Deployment, Service, Gateway or Ingress, and managed TLS where
practical.
2. Add Network Policy, PodDisruptionBudget, topology spread, resource requests, and graceful shutdown.
3. Configure HPA with a measurable target and define dependency-safe maximum replicas.
4. Generate load and capture scale-up latency, errors, pod scheduling, and dependency behavior.

VOLUME 8D | 12
5. Perform a rolling update and a failed canary; demonstrate rollback.
6. Simulate one failure: pod crash, node drain, denied network path, or bad readiness probe.
7. Create a fleet/policy/backup design for scaling this platform across clusters. Validation Evidence

Traffic reaches only healthy endpoints.

Scaling evidence includes application and dependency metrics.

The failed release is detected and rolled back.

The incident timeline links symptom to Kubernetes and infrastructure evidence. Cleanup

Delete application, gateway/load balancer, policies, backup objects, and cluster if dedicated. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why can HPA fail even when configured correctly?
Metrics, resource requests, pod startup time, scheduler capacity, quotas, and dependency limits can prevent
safe scaling.
2. What is the purpose of a PDB?
It limits voluntary disruption of available replicas; it does not guarantee availability during every failure.
3. Why use Gateway API?
It separates infrastructure and application roles and supports richer, portable traffic-management resources.
4. What does a GKE fleet provide?
A logical grouping for consistent identity, policy, configuration, service, and multi-cluster management
capabilities. Chapter Summary

Production GKE operations cross Kubernetes and Google Cloud layers.

Autoscaling requires dependency and cost guardrails.

Fleets standardize multi-cluster governance but do not replace architecture.

Troubleshooting should follow the request path and evidence chain.

Chapter 34 - Cloud Run Services, Jobs, and Worker Pools
Running containers without managing Kubernetes while preserving production controls
Learning Objectives

Select Cloud Run services, jobs, or worker pools from execution semantics.

Engineer revisions, traffic splitting, concurrency, autoscaling, and rollback.

Design private networking, service identity, secrets, and authenticated invocation.

Operate cost, cold starts, background work, and multi-region resilience.
34.1 Resource Models
Cloud Run is a fully managed application platform for code, functions, and containers. Services expose request-
driven endpoints and autoscale. Jobs run tasks to completion. Worker pools run continuous background work
without a load-balanced URL and, according to current documentation, do not provide automatic scaling. Choose from lifecycle semantics, not deployment convenience. Resource

34.2 Revisions, Traffic, and Scaling
Every configuration or image change creates a revision. Split traffic between revisions for canaries, migrate
gradually, and retain known-good revisions for rollback. Concurrency determines how many requests one
instance can serve; minimum instances reduce cold-start risk; maximum instances protect cost and
downstream systems.
gcloud run deploy orders --image=REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/apps/orders@sha256:DIGEST --region=REGION --no-allow-
unauthenticated
gcloud run services update-traffic orders --region=REGION --to-revisions=orders-00042=10,orders-00041=90
34.3 Identity, Ingress, and VPC Connectivity
Use a dedicated service identity with least privilege. Keep services private unless public access is an explicit
requirement. Ingress settings control accepted network paths; IAM controls who can invoke. Direct VPC egress
lets services and jobs reach VPC resources without managing a Serverless VPC Access connector, and network
tags can support granular firewall rules. Worker pools can use Direct VPC ingress and egress.

Use Secret Manager references rather than plaintext environment variables for secrets.

Use authenticated service-to-service invocation with identity tokens.

Separate public frontend, internal API, batch, and worker identities.

Control egress and DNS so private dependencies are reachable without broad internet access.

34.4 Reliability, Cost, and Multi-Region Design
Cloud Run services are regional. Multi-region designs use independent services, global application delivery,
health-based routing, replicated state, and tested failover. Scale-to-zero saves cost but can add latency. Minimum instances, CPU allocation, concurrency, timeouts, and retries must be tuned together. Never let
automatic scale overwhelm a database or third-party API. Troubleshooting Matrix

Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. How do services and jobs differ?
Services handle requests and autoscale; jobs execute finite tasks to completion with task-level retries.
2. Why set maximum instances?
To bound cost and protect downstream systems from unbounded autoscaling.
3. What is a Cloud Run revision?
An immutable version of a service configuration and container image used for traffic management and
rollback.
4. When use a worker pool?
For continuous background processing without a public endpoint when explicitly managed capacity is
acceptable. Chapter Summary

Cloud Run offers distinct service, job, worker, and function execution models.

Revisions make gradual delivery and rollback first-class.

IAM, ingress, and VPC controls are separate layers.

Autoscaling must be bounded by dependency capacity and cost.

Chapter 35 - Cloud Run Functions and Event-Driven Compute
Engineering small event handlers with production reliability and lifecycle controls
Learning Objectives

Use current Cloud Run functions terminology and deployment models.

Design HTTP and CloudEvents handlers with idempotency and bounded retries.

Secure function identity, ingress, secrets, and dependencies.

Choose functions, Cloud Run services, jobs, or Workflows appropriately.
35.1 Current Function Model
Cloud Functions (2nd gen) is now Cloud Run functions. Existing Cloud Functions v2 APIs and gcloud functions
workflows remain available for compatibility, but Google recommends transitioning to functions in Cloud Run. Functions use language frameworks and can receive HTTP requests or CloudEvents from supported event
sources. Choice
Strength
When to Reconsider

Minimal single-purpose handler
Complex container/runtime control or
many endpoints

Only a tiny handler is required

Immediate request/event response is
required

Heavy compute or custom runtime logic
35.2 Idempotency and Event Semantics
Events can be redelivered. Use a stable event or business key, store processing state atomically, and make side
effects conditional. Acknowledging before durable completion loses work; retrying non-idempotent effects
duplicates work.

redelivered. Use a stable event or business key, store processing state atomically, and make side
effects conditional. Acknowledging before durable completion loses work; retrying non-idempotent effects
duplicates work. Poison events need bounded retry and dead-letter or quarantine handling.

Validate event type, source, subject, schema, and size.

Record event ID and processing outcome with expiration where appropriate.

Use transactional outbox/inbox or conditional writes for critical effects.

Separate transient errors from permanent validation failures.
35.3 Security and Dependency Controls
Each function needs a dedicated runtime identity. Restrict invocation and ingress, use Secret Manager, and
avoid embedding credentials. Cap instances and concurrency to protect databases. Network private
dependencies through supported Cloud Run networking, and avoid unrestricted egress for sensitive handlers.
